submissions.findingTextShort: A nine-person food study shows dose-dependent gastric re-acidification with Betaine HCl, but not digestive clinical efficacy or a validated consumer regimen.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 31485804 used an open-label randomized four-period crossover in nine healthy participants to test Betaine HCl after food raised gastric pH. Doses of 1500, 3000, and 4500 mg were studied, with 4500 mg restoring baseline gastric pH faster after food. This is transient gastric-pH physiology under the studied meal context; it does not establish benefit for dyspepsia, malabsorption, reflux, nutrient status, or a routine 4500 mg consumer dose.
submissions.populationContext: Nine healthy participants in an acute meal-associated crossover physiology study
submissions.usageContext: Betaine hydrochloride gastric-pH physiology; not anhydrous betaine and not digestive-outcome efficacy
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Very small sample, acute exposure, meal dependence, and surrogate physiology limit clinical inference and repeated-use dosing conclusions.

submissions.findingTextShort: Betaine HCl can alter exposure to a pH-sensitive drug under induced hypochlorhydria; this is a drug-specific PK interaction, not a generic absorption benefit.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 25274610 studied healthy volunteers with rabeprazole-induced hypochlorhydria and found that 1500 mg Betaine HCl rapidly re-acidified the stomach and substantially restored exposure of the pH-sensitive drug dasatinib. The result demonstrates a deliberate drug-pharmacokinetic interaction under a specific acid-suppression, timing, and formulation context. It cannot be generalized into improved nutrient absorption, universal drug-absorption rescue, or broad digestive efficacy.
submissions.populationContext: Healthy volunteers under experimentally induced hypochlorhydria
submissions.usageContext: Drug-, timing-, and pH-dependent pharmacokinetic interaction
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The result is specific to the studied drug and induced-acid-suppression protocol; direction and magnitude can differ for other drugs and conditions.

submissions.findingTextShort: A fed atazanavir study found only limited recovery of drug exposure with 1500 mg Betaine HCl, constraining blanket absorption-rescue claims.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 28028768 evaluated 1500 mg Betaine HCl with atazanavir/ritonavir in a fed crossover under rabeprazole-induced hypochlorhydria. Betaine HCl restored only a small fraction of the acid-suppression-associated loss in atazanavir exposure. This directly contradicts any claim that gastric re-acidification reliably normalizes absorption for all pH-sensitive drugs and reinforces drug-, meal-, timing-, and formulation-specific interpretation.
submissions.populationContext: Human fed crossover under induced hypochlorhydria
submissions.uncertaintyNote: One drug context does not define all interactions, but the limited rescue must remain first-class evidence against universalization.

submissions.findingTextShort: A published evidence review describes limited clinical data for Betaine HCl and notes that common empirical meal-time dose escalation has not been rigorously tested for outcomes.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 32549862 reviewed Betaine HCl for functional hypochlorhydria and noted that it is widely recommended despite limited published evidence. The commonly described empirical meal-time dose-escalation protocol has not been rigorously validated for clinical outcomes. Transient gastric-pH effects therefore cannot close evidence gaps for dyspepsia, reflux, malabsorption, nutrient status, long-term safety, or an evidence-based chronic dosing protocol.
submissions.usageContext: Clinical-evidence and dosing-governance gap for Betaine hydrochloride
submissions.uncertaintyNote: A review can identify evidence limitations but does not prove absence of benefit; proposition-compatible outcome trials remain required.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2025 review found selected high-intensity signals for creatine plus beta-alanine, but additive benefit over single supplements was inconsistent and absent for several domains.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 40647180 systematically reviewed seven randomized controlled trials involving 263 participants receiving creatine plus beta-alanine. Combination evidence was most favorable for selected high-intensity or anaerobic outcomes, while additive effects over appropriate single-supplement comparators were inconsistent; no consistent additional benefit was established for maximal strength, body composition, aerobic capacity, or broad athletic performance. Combination-versus-placebo benefit must not be relabeled as synergy.
submissions.populationContext: Participants across seven randomized controlled combination trials
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Heterogeneous protocols, doses, training status, endpoints and comparators limit generalization; preserve favorable and null domains together.

submissions.findingTextShort: A four-group placebo/creatine/beta-alanine/combination trial found no significant group effect for VO2peak, time to exhaustion, or threshold outcomes.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 16953366 was a double-blind placebo-controlled four-group study in 55 men comparing placebo, creatine, beta-alanine, and their combination for four weeks. Despite some within-group changes, no significant between-group effects were found for VO2peak, time to exhaustion, or threshold-related endpoints. This direct comparator trial is evidence against broad aerobic-endurance or universal additive-efficacy claims for the fixed combination.
submissions.populationContext: 55 men in a four-week four-arm controlled supplementation trial
submissions.usageContext: Direct single-supplement and combination comparator evidence
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Null aerobic findings do not exclude effects on other task domains, but they must not be dropped when summarizing combination performance evidence.

submissions.findingTextShort: A four-group repeated-Wingate study does not support converting oxidative-stress biomarker changes into simple combination performance efficacy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 27217925 randomized 44 sedentary men for 28 days to placebo, creatine, beta-alanine, or the combination during repeated Wingate testing. Oxidative-stress and related biomarker outcomes did not show a simple combination advantage. Mechanistic or biomarker changes from this trial must remain distinct from functional performance efficacy, and the sedentary male population and training context must remain attached.
submissions.populationContext: 44 sedentary men in a 28-day four-arm randomized study
submissions.usageContext: Biomarker/mechanistic outcomes versus functional efficacy boundary
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Biomarker endpoints are not interchangeable with performance endpoints and should not be promoted into broad benefit claims.

submissions.findingTextShort: A tiny male-military trial found selected benefits after adding short creatine loading to prior beta-alanine exposure, with several null biochemical outcomes.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 35805647 randomized 20 male military personnel after three weeks of beta-alanine to beta-alanine plus seven days of creatine loading at 0.3 g/kg/day versus beta-alanine plus placebo. Selected strength, jump, sprint or casualty-evacuation, and mathematical-processing outcomes favored the creatine-added condition, while several hormonal and biochemical outcomes were null. The unequal constituent exposure sequence, tiny male-military population, short creatine-loading window, and endpoint specificity prevent this study from establishing general synergy or a universal combination regimen.
submissions.populationContext: 20 male military personnel after prior beta-alanine exposure
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Because both groups were already receiving beta-alanine and only creatine was newly randomized, this design does not estimate a clean de-novo fixed-combination effect in a general population.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 network meta-analysis found no synergistic or additional performance advantage for creatine plus beta-alanine beyond creatine monotherapy across evaluated domains.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 42384726, DOI 10.1080/15502783.2026.2695133, was a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis of 52 randomized controlled trials examining creatine, beta-alanine, and their combination in healthy adult athletes. The synthesis reported no synergistic advantage for co-supplementation; creatine alone produced the most consistent high-intensity or anaerobic effects, while the combination did not add benefit beyond creatine monotherapy across the evaluated performance domains. This newer synthesis must be preserved alongside, not substituted for, the somewhat more favorable 2025 review PMID 40647180.
submissions.populationContext: Healthy adult athletes represented across 52 randomized controlled trials
submissions.usageContext: Network-level comparative synthesis of creatine, beta-alanine and combination interventions
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Network meta-analysis includes indirect comparisons and heterogeneous protocols; task domain, trial duration, dose and direct-versus-indirect comparator structure remain material. The result constrains synergy claims rather than proving no possible context-specific benefit.
